To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the offspring of overweight and obese mothers are at a greater risk of being obese in adulthood.
Maternal overweight and obesity in early pregnancy and 21-year post-partum are associated with increased odds of offspring overweight and obesity at 21 year post-partum.
maternal BMI changes over two decades are associated with offspring BMI at 2 decades.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between change of maternal body mass index and offspring body mass index.
the impact of maternal weight status over a long period of time on their offspring’s weight status.
maternal weight change and its effect on offspring weight.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
maternal weight gain from pre-pregnant to two decades post-pregnancy is associated with an increase in offspring BMI.
maternal overweight and obesity is a risk factor for offspring overweight and obesity, and this risk is increased by the persistence of maternal overweight and obesity over two decades.
a mother’s BMI before pregnancy and the changes that occur over time in the mother’s BMI are important factors in the development of obesity in her offspring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of obesity in offspring is increased by the persistence of maternal obesity, and by a change in maternal BMI, from normal to overweight or obese.
the offspring of women who become overweight or remain overweight are more likely to be at risk of overweight and obesity in adulthood.
maternal overweight and obesity are important predictors of offspring overweight and obesity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of overweight or obesity in the offspring is increased by maternal weight gain over the long term.
women should be encouraged to maintain their weight before pregnancy and during the postpartum period to reduce the risk of obesity in their offspring.
the risk of obesity in the offspring is increased by a persistently overweight maternal BMI, rather than by an increase in BMI from normal to overweight.
